incidents.what_happened: In a 14 August 2026 letter to the Lake Wynonah Property Owners Association, Kirk Kreider, acting chief of PADEP's Division of Dam Safety, declared the 1971 earthen Lake Wynonah Dam 'unsafe' and requested an immediate voluntary full drawdown of the 175-acre reservoir at up to one foot per day, with a formal order threatened if the association does not comply. The letter cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway, inability to pass a major flood, and temporary bracing of the top walls after a spillway collapse at the community's Fawn Lake Dam. incidents.what_happened: The Lawrence Journal-World reported on 13 August 2026 that one of four inflatable rubber bladders on the crest of Bowersock Dam had been punctured by heavy floating debris and ripped from end to end. Co-owner Sarah Hill-Nelson said the No. 2 bladder failure left a gap that dropped the upstream millpond about six feet. The concrete dam was holding; there was no downstream flood wave. The city of Lawrence said the Kaw River Water Treatment Plant continued to operate, though low pond levels are less efficient for intake and filtration. The run-of-river dam supplies Kansas's only hydroelectric plant and maintains the pond for the city's water intake. Hill-Nelson said a replacement bladder would take about four months and cost upwards of $300,000, and that this was the first time a Lawrence bladder had been destroyed beyond repair (a 2021 seam tear had been stitched). Exact calendar day of the puncture was described only as recently before the Thursday 13 August article.
incidents.status: Concrete dam intact; No. 2 inflatable crest bladder destroyed; millpond about six feet below normal; water plant operating; repair approach undecided as of 13 August 2026.

incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened a levee breach more than 40 metres wide on the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan, on the night of Wednesday 12 August 2026; more than 2,000 people were relocated and Xinhua reported no casualties. That breach was sealed on Friday night 14 August after nearly two days of sandbagging, because heavy plant could not reach the narrow levee crown. A separate eastern-embankment breach on the Jialu River in Chuanhui District, Zhoukou, opened around 23:00 on Thursday 13 August, widening from about 30 metres to about 117 metres under Jialu inflows and Shaying River backwater. China Daily and People's Daily/Xinhua said the Jialu breach was sealed on Saturday night 15 August after more than 2,000 emergency personnel worked the site; crews continued raising, reinforcing and sealing seepage. A Level-IV national disaster-relief response was activated for Henan.

incidents.what_happened: Intense rain on the night of 2 August 2026 flooded the Laurel Fork area of Carroll County. Virginia DCR Regional Engineer Steven Bricker observed on 4 August that the Olde Mill Golf Club lake (normal pool near 300 acre-feet) was almost completely drained after a partial breach. DCR's 5 August letter to owner Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC stated the primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser and significant sediment loss; the dam has a preliminary high-hazard classification and may not impound water until corrective action. incidents.cause_summary: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026.
incidents.what_happened: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir in Hengzhou to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026. Nanning raised flood-control emergency response to Level I; CCTV video showed a large release through the dam breach. At a 9 July news conference, Nanning Vice-Mayor Ding Wei said the Liulan breach had caused 26 deaths (5 then unidentified) and 7 people missing, while Guangxi overall had 39 dead and 9 missing — figures that could overlap pending DNA identification. Deputy water-resources director Zhai Jianjia said Liulan water had fallen below dam-foundation rock, the breach and discharge had largely stabilised, and crest access was restored that morning for dredging. A major incident was declared. About 1,500 residents of Whaley Bridge, Furness Vale and New Mills were evacuated for up to six nights. Emergency drawdown used high-volume pumps; an RAF Chinook dropped hundreds of tonnes of aggregate onto the damaged chute. Independent reviews by Prof. David Balmforth (government) and Dr Andrew Hughes (owner) found inherent 1970 design flaws. No deaths. Permanent repairs were still underway into 2025.
incidents.status: Dam stabilised after emergency works; multi-year reconstruction of a new spillway, with refill expected over winter 2025–26.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 1,500 residents evacuated for up to six nights

incidents.name: Columbia Canal embankment (Congaree / Broad River diversion)
incidents.location_label: Columbia Canal near the municipal water plant, Columbia, South Carolina
incidents.geo_source: Columbia Canal / SC State Museum riverfront; NWS locates the breach on the canal that feeds the city water plant
incidents.river_or_facility: Columbia Canal (Broad–Congaree diversion)
incidents.cause_summary: Record Congaree/Broad flood overtopped and tore the historic canal dike that feeds Columbia's water-treatment plant.
incidents.what_happened: The Columbia Canal, a 19th-century diversion that takes Broad River water along the Congaree riverfront to Columbia's water plant and a small hydro station, breached during the 1–5 October 2015 flood. The NWS service assessment dates the breach 3 October; The State later described a roughly 60-foot tear before dawn on 5 October and a second dike collapse that week. Canal level dropped so fast that the city had to pump Broad River water into the plant reservoir. National Guard helicopters dropped hundreds of one-ton sandbags into the gap. About half of the Columbia water system's ~375,000 customers were at risk of losing supply. The canal is a separate structure from the Gills Creek pond dams that failed the same week.
incidents.status: historical / emergency sandbag and later FEMA-funded embankment repair (DR-4241)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Columbia water system ~375,000 customers at risk; boil-water / conservation orders

incidents.name: Boone Dam (karst sinkhole and seepage)
incidents.location_label: Boone Dam on the South Fork Holston River, Tennessee
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Boone Dam 36°26′24″N 82°26′16″W
incidents.river_or_facility: Boone Dam / Boone Lake (TVA)
incidents.cause_summary: A sinkhole and turbid seepage at the downstream toe in October 2014 showed internal erosion through the karst foundation; TVA drew the lake down and later built a composite seepage barrier.
incidents.what_happened: During an informal inspection on 20 October 2014, TVA staff found a sinkhole at the downstream toe of Boone Dam's earth embankment, then turbid seepage into the tailrace. The dam itself did not breach. TVA repaired the hole, built a tailrace filter, closed the reservation, instrumented the dam, and dropped Boone Lake about 10 ft below winter pool. Investigation showed soil loss in infilled karst under the embankment. TVA chose a grout curtain plus concrete diaphragm wall from the crest into rock. Interim low-pool operations lasted years. No uncontrolled release and no deaths.
incidents.status: historical / composite seepage barrier constructed; reservoir later returned toward normal operations

incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (2014 Dan River coal ash spill)
incidents.river_or_facility: Dan River Steam Station ash pond / Dan River
incidents.cause_summary: A 48-inch storm drain pipe under a 27-acre ash pond collapsed (EPA: limited structural flaw). Pipe left unsealed for almost a week.
incidents.what_happened: On 2 February 2014 a drainage pipe burst under a Duke Energy coal-ash pond at the closed Dan River Steam Station in Eden, NC. Wikipedia: 39,000 tons of coal ash and 27 million gallons of wastewater entered the Dan River; ash deposited up to 70 miles downstream. WISE: about 82,000 short tons (74,400 t) of ash and 100,000 m³ of water. No deaths. Duke later pleaded guilty to Clean Water Act counts and paid large federal/state fines (Wikipedia: $102 million federal criminal fine among others). EPA oversaw cleanup.
incidents.status: Release stopped after about six days; long-term ash-pond closure ordered in North Carolina.

incidents.name: Carriage Hills No. 2 Dam (Estes Park)
incidents.location_label: Fish Creek drainage, Estes Park, Colorado

incidents.cause_summary: The town-owned lower Carriage Hills dam overtopped and failed overnight 12–13 September 2013 when Fish Creek peaked at about five times the 100-year flow.
incidents.what_happened: During the 9–18 September 2013 Front Range storm, Fish Creek through Estes Park ran at roughly five times a 100-year peak (NRCS). Both town-owned Carriage Hills dams overtopped on 12 September. Colorado Dam Safety's forensic note puts failure of the lower (No. 2) dam around 22:00 on the 12th or 02:00–03:00 on the 13th. The floodway had been evacuated. ASDSO and the state after-action report list Carriage Hills #2 among nine low-hazard dams that failed; no additional deaths or major extra property loss were attributed to this breach beyond the flood itself. Carriage Hills No. 1 overtopped but is not listed as failed.

incidents.region: Ia Krel commune, Đức Cơ district, Gia Lai

incidents.cause_summary: The new earth dam was built without the specified concrete face and was filled before acceptance; it failed during first filling.
incidents.what_happened: Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade and Gia Lai investigators found that Ia Krel 2, a 5.5 MW scheme started in 2010 by Bảo Long–Gia Lai, began storing water in May 2013 and that a section of the main dam broke about 05:00 on 12 June. incidents.name: Brown Bridge Dam (temporary dewatering structure)
incidents.location_label: Boardman River south of Traverse City, Michigan
incidents.river_or_facility: Brown Bridge Dam / TDS on the Boardman River
incidents.cause_summary: On first loading of a temporary drawdown channel built for dam removal, foundation soils piped under the control slab and the adjacent embankment collapsed, emptying Brown Bridge Pond in hours.
incidents.what_happened: The City of Traverse City was removing the 1921 Brown Bridge hydro dam on the Boardman River. A steel-sheetpile temporary dewatering structure (TDS) was built beside the spillway to lower the 191-acre pond over about two weeks. On the morning of 6 October 2012, at first loading, a boil appeared downstream of the channel slab. Flow under the slab scoured foundation soils; the embankment between the TDS and the old spillway collapsed. The pond emptied in about 4–6 hours instead of weeks. About 66 downstream properties were damaged. Michigan EGLE / MDEQ later concluded internal erosion of foundation material under the control section. No deaths.
incidents.status: historical / dam removal later completed; pond not restored
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 66 properties damaged (ASDSO / MDEQ)

incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain overtopped the earthen dam. Later commentary cited inadequate spillway design and ignored consultant warnings from the 1960s. Six other dams failed the same night; only Sandy Run also killed people (5).
incidents.what_happened: At 02:35 on 20 July 1977, during the Johnstown flood, Laurel Run Dam No. 2 failed, releasing 101 million US gallons down a 3-mile valley into Tanneryville. Forty people died, 9 homes were destroyed and 19 damaged. There was no warning system; most residents were asleep. Damage about $5.3 million. The dam was never rebuilt; the site is now Laurel Run Park.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Tanneryville: 9 homes destroyed, 19 damaged

incidents.name: Euclides da Cunha and Limoeiro (Armando de Salles Oliveira) dams
incidents.region: São José do Rio Pardo and Mococa, São Paulo
incidents.location_label: Rio Pardo cascade, São José do Rio Pardo, São Paulo, Brazil
incidents.geo_source: Global Energy Monitor Euclides da Cunha plant −21.6031, −46.9492
incidents.river_or_facility: UHE Euclides da Cunha and UHE Limoeiro on the Rio Pardo
incidents.cause_summary: Gates at Euclides da Cunha were not opened in time during a cloudburst; the earth dam overtopped and the flood then breached Limoeiro 10–12 km downstream.
incidents.what_happened: Portuguese Wikipedia and a USU cascade-failure paper describe the 19–20 January 1977 Rio Pardo disaster. After three weeks of rain and about 180 mm in 24 hours, CESP operators did not open Euclides da Cunha's floodgates in time (Gazeta do Rio Pardo later quoted a witness that an earlier operator had been sacked for opening gates without São Paulo's leave). Overtopping began about 20:30 on 19 January; the 56 m earth dam breached about 03:30 on the 20th, some 100 m from the right abutment, releasing more than 13 million m³. About 30 minutes later the 35 m Limoeiro / Salles de Oliveira dam 10 km downstream also failed, adding about 25 million m³. Folha de S.Paulo's 21 January 1977 front page said the river broke four dams and flooded nine towns. Both plants were rebuilt; Euclides da Cunha now has 108.8 MW.
incidents.status: Both dams reconstructed; plants operating (now Auren Energia).
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Nine towns flooded (Folha de S.Paulo, 21 Jan 1977); no official death toll in sources fetched

incidents.what_happened: The Bureau of Reclamation earthfill Teton Dam failed during first filling on 5 June 1976 after seepage and piping through the abutment and core. incidents.name: Roppadammen / Roppdammen (Nordre Ropptjern)
incidents.region: Innlandet (then Oppland) / Gausdal kommune, Vestre Gausdal / Bødal
incidents.location_label: Gausdal, Norway

incidents.cause_summary: NTH professor Ragnar Heggstad: breach at the bottom outlet. First filling autumn 1975 was incomplete because of drought; an ice cap around the bottom outlet later melted and water entered the moraine fill. NVE Project Dam Safety later cites Roppa 1976 as a leakage/piping failure. Eyewitness saw a hole under the dam / an emergency gate in the basin rim wash out.
incidents.what_happened: The newly built intake embankment at Nordre Ropptjern failed on Constitution Day. Farm Sagsveen was totally destroyed; Svea dwelling house was taken; 100 m of Rv 255 foundation and Forsetbrua on Jøra were damaged. No human deaths; livestock losses uncertain. Sheriff warned at 12:10 and rescued another elderly couple.
incidents.status: failure; dam rebuilt; power station commissioned 1977

incidents.name: Old River Control Low Sill (1973 Mississippi flood)
incidents.location_label: Old River Control Complex, lower Mississippi River, Louisiana
incidents.geo_source: Old River Control Structure complex on the Mississippi–Atchafalaya connection
incidents.river_or_facility: Old River Control Low-Sill Structure
incidents.cause_summary: The 1973 Mississippi flood undermined the low-sill structure; a wing wall failed and emergency rock was dumped to keep the river from jumping into the Atchafalaya.
incidents.what_happened: USACE's Old River Control Complex, completed in 1963, is meant to keep about 70 percent of combined Mississippi–Red flow in the main river and 30 percent in the Atchafalaya. In the 1973 flood the low-sill structure was loaded far above design. Scour and piping under the stilling basin and a wing-wall failure put the structure at risk of losing the river. Barges of rock were sunk and dumped to armor the foundation. The river did not avulse. USACE later added the Auxiliary Structure (1986) so the low sill would never again take the whole load. No deaths at the structure. This is a named near-loss of the lower Mississippi alignment, not a reservoir-dam collapse.
incidents.status: historical / low sill repaired; Auxiliary Structure added 1986

In Kings County at least 12 highway bridges were carried away or badly damaged. The same official write-up states, without naming the structures, that two dams at the Head of Millstream were lost. Wikipedia (Fraser River) lists that date as the first of a sequence of named lower-valley dyke failures. The Chilliwack Progress, citing the Chilliwack Museum's flood history, says that on 28 May the Mission gauge reached 23.05 feet (7 m) and there was a major break in the Semiault dike, which was soon repaired; later small breaks occurred again as the Cannor dyke failed. The Weather Network's 1948 anniversary piece also dates the Semiault Creek dike break to Friday 28 May, before the Glendale and Cannor failures already recorded separately. Legion Magazine published a Chilliwack Museum photograph of volunteers repairing the dike on Semiault Creek, a Fraser tributary. Regional 1948 deaths (often given as 10) are not copied onto this named dyke.
incidents.status: Repaired in 1948; Fraser Valley dykes later widened and heightened.

incidents.name: Moutoa floodway southern stopbank (trestle bridge)

incidents.cause_summary: Court of Appeal (Easton Agriculture, 2013): after the Moutoa sluice gates were opened, the southern floodway stopbank failed at a trestle bridge; the Sutherland review blamed the bridge–stopbank interaction.
incidents.what_happened: On 16 February 2004 Horizons (then Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council) opened the Moutoa sluice gates at 07:00 to relieve the Manawatū River. The New Zealand Court of Appeal in Easton Agriculture Ltd v Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council [2013] NZCA 79 found that during the night of 16–17 February the southern stopbank of the Moutoa floodway failed at a trestle bridge: a farmer saw an upstream breach about 03:20 on 17 February; further breaches were seen at 05:30; and at 06:30 a 'catastrophic' blow-out occurred downstream of the bridge. The breach reached 23 m upstream and 17 m downstream of the bridge centreline; the bridge itself stayed intact. Floodwater covered the Moutoa Basin and the appellants' farms for about 12 days. The council's Sutherland Report said the likely cause was interaction between the bridge structure and the stopbank. Te Ara records that the February 2004 flood was the largest on the Manawatū since 1902 and that a number of Lower Manawatū Scheme stopbank failures inundated about 25% of the protected area. No source attached a death count to this breach.
incidents.status: Stopbank repaired; scheme upgrades after 2004.

incidents.name: Matahina Dam (1967 first-filling cavity)
incidents.region: Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty, North Island
incidents.location_label: Matahina Dam right abutment, Rangitāiki River, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand

incidents.river_or_facility: Matahina Dam, Rangitāiki River
incidents.cause_summary: First filling cracked the core and inner transition against an unremoved abutment bench; a pipe developed and an erosion cavity appeared on the downstream right abutment.
incidents.what_happened: Matahina, a rockfill dam with a rolled silt core on the Rangitāiki, was filled in late 1966–early 1967. ISSMGE (Gillon and Newton, citing Galloway 1967): after the lake was held on the spillway at RL 66 m, filling from 5 January raised the lake to RL 74.7 m in six days and to RL 76.2 m on 22 January; large leakage then appeared in the underdrain. About two weeks later a subsidence was found on the downstream side of the core at the right abutment. A shaft 8.5 × 6.1 m in plan was taken 16.5 m down to RL 63 m and revealed a 1.8 m construction bench at RL 67.4 m that had not been removed, plus a 200 mm pipe into the downstream rockfill; material loss was estimated at more than 100 m³. International Water Power and Wikipedia describe the same first-filling cavity, lake lowering, and core repair with a plastic-concrete patch and filter backfill. The repair performed until the separate 2 March 1987 Edgecumbe earthquake incident (already drafted). Engineering papers and the official NZ dam-incident series record no fatalities.
incidents.status: Core repaired 1967; later damaged again in the 1987 earthquake (separate record).

incidents.status: Historical TSF breach. Town later rebuilt around surviving church and mine museum.

incidents.cause_summary: EA: a rapidly deepening crest-road depression on 7 March 1983 sat above a sharp concrete/puddle-clay interface; voids in the puddle core were grouted after a 9.3 m drawdown.
incidents.what_happened: On the afternoon of 7 March 1983 a member of the public walking dogs noticed a depression in the asphalt of the crest roadway of the 35 m Greenbooth Dam, about 20 m from the west abutment. The EA report: by mid-morning the next day it measured 3 m by 1 m and had subsided 0.16 m, directly above the toe of a concrete wing wall where the concrete/puddle-clay interface changed direction sharply. incidents.status: Grouted and returned to service; still a United Utilities reservoir.

incidents.cause_summary: Czech Wikipedia / Brdy local history: dam on unstable Cambrian bedrock with seepage during first filling; after long rains the embankment breached the night of 21–22 June 1854.
incidents.what_happened: Pilská (Sofiin) reservoir above Příbram, built 1849–1853 by the Klein brothers for mine and smelter water, failed shortly after completion. Czech Wikipedia: after long rains the dam fully breached before midnight on 21 June 1854; the flood caused heavy damage in Bohutín and killed two people. A contemporary Příbram mining account (Solvayovy lomy text) dates the night to 22 June 1854, says the ~20 m dam reached 16.2 m, and likewise records two deaths, with riders sent down the Litavka to warn people. The dam was repaired 1854–1861; later reconstructions followed more seepage. Two deaths in Bohutín are the dam-flood figure used here.
incidents.status: Rebuilt and later reconstructed; now a Příbram drinking-water reservoir.

incidents.name: Mladotický rybník (Mlatzer Teich)
incidents.location_label: Mladotice, Plzeň Region, Czechia
incidents.geo_source: German Wikipedia list of dam accidents (Mlatzer Teich) 49°58′15.4″N 13°20′55.6″E
incidents.river_or_facility: Mladotický rybník / Mladotický potok / Střela
incidents.cause_summary: Czech Wikipedia: extreme cloudburst filled the pond; the outlet was not opened in time and could not later be reached; the dam then burst in two places.
incidents.what_happened: On 25 May 1872 an extreme cloudburst hit western Bohemia (a priest at Žebnice measured 237 mm in about 90 minutes). Czech Wikipedia (Mladotický rybník): the large pond (then the largest in western Bohemia, about 91–92 ha) filled; the outlet was not opened in time; the dam cracked in two places during the night of 25–26 May and water entered the already flooded Střela. Ekolist / hydrologist Bohumír Janský: up to about 3.5 million m3 left the pond. Povodí Ohře: the Střela rise was mainly from this breach. The pond was not restored; a landslide a day or two later created Odlezelské Lake (a different event). The May 1872 Berounka flash flood as a whole killed on the order of 240–244 people across many municipalities — that regional flood toll is not applied to this dam.
incidents.status: Not rebuilt; former pond floor is now an educational trail.

incidents.what_happened: The Ibra earth dam at Kirchheim (built mid-1970s as a recreation lake) failed at 15:25 on 22 August 1977 during a storm, still in the trial-filling period. incidents.what_happened: During the 21 June 1984 Fronleichnamsflut the small Gissigheim earth flood-retention dam (late 1950s; about 9.7 m; ordinary storage 144,000 m3) overtopped from about 16:00 and breached about 17:20. The dam was not rebuilt (remains later removed).

incidents.cause_summary: Bornschein and Pohl (IAHR 2003) and Daigner: undersized spillway and freeboard; bottom outlet blocked by debris; crest overtopped about 90 minutes, then the earth dam breached beside the spillway.
incidents.what_happened: The small green flood-retention basin above Glashütte (built 1951–53; original storage about 50,000 m3) failed during the 12 August 2002 Saxony flood. incidents.what_happened: The Tiefosi earth dam in Shangcheng County, Henan, failed on 17 May 1960 while still under construction. Adevarul: during first filling, large seepage under the foundation block (over 150 L/s) and displacements at the contact between the central arch and the left-bank parabolic wing were observed. incidents.name: Siburúa Dam
incidents.region: South of Coro, near Meachiche / Siburúa, Falcón (Sierra de San Luis)

incidents.river_or_facility: Embalse Siburúa (off-stream, fed by sierra springs)
incidents.cause_summary: Suárez Villar compilation and a Venezuelan earth-dam review: a deep downstream-slope slide in a homogeneous clay section near the abutment while the reservoir was full, after a 1959 rapid-drawdown slide on the upstream face. Wolfskill and Lambe (1969) attributed the slides to brittle medium-plasticity clays.
incidents.what_happened: Embalse Siburúa is a small off-stream earth dam south of Coro, Falcón, built 1956–1957 to supply oil facilities on the Paraguaná Peninsula (technical book: zoned at the highest section, homogeneous near the abutments; maximum height 16 m; reservoir 615,000 m³). A 1959 rapid drawdown produced an upstream-slope slide. In 1964, with the reservoir full, a deep slide occurred on the downstream face near the hillside, forcing a complete drawdown. Laboratory and stability work by Wolfskill and Lambe in 1969 found brittle medium-plasticity clays. The dam was left out of service after El Isiro entered operation. Suárez Villar / Frontiers (2020) list it among Venezuela’s seven historic dam failures (slope slippage, 1964) and state that El Guapo is the only Venezuelan dam failure with recorded loss of life.
incidents.status: Abandoned after 1964; out of service.

incidents.what_happened: El Cristo is a homogeneous medium/high-plasticity clay embankment on the Río El Cristo northwest of Mirimire, Falcón (official 2011 Falcón environmental fiche: height 22.4 m; crest 209 m; maximum storage 15.92 hm³; buried rectangular spillway 3×2 m, design discharge 9.23 m³/s; built 1980–1987 for potable supply). incidents.what_happened: Manuelote (Embalse Socuy) is a zoned earth dam on the Río Socuy about 100 km northwest of Maracaibo (Tekhné: main dam height 34.3 m, crest 1,300 m at 56.00 m asl; homogeneous earth closure dike 13.5 m × 1,600 m; built mid-1970s by MOP for Maracaibo / El Tablazo supply and flood control). On 5 December 2010 an exceptional Socuy flood raised the pool almost to the crest. Witnesses told Tekhné the water did not overtop at the breach — about 8 cm below — then the closure dike collapsed suddenly by regressive erosion, cutting a gully that emptied most of the reservoir and stopped transfers to Tulé. Peak outflow was estimated at about 2,200 m³/s. Vice-president Elías Jaua (AVN, 5 Dec 2010) said the 35 m / 266 million m³ dam had given way, about 300 people were evacuated from the nearest hamlet, and there was no loss of life. Frontiers (2020) lists Manuelote among Venezuela’s seven historic dam failures and states El Guapo is the only Venezuelan dam failure with recorded fatalities.

incidents.what_happened: Penn Forest Dam, an earthfill water-supply dam 145 feet high and 1,930 feet long built 1956–58 for Bethlehem, developed about 350 gpm seepage from a downstream road as first filling reached 4.5 feet below the spillway in 1960. In July 1994 piezometers near the original sinkhole dropped 10–20 feet and seepage exceeded 900 gpm; the dam was drawn down 25 feet and replaced by an RCC gravity dam completed in 1998. No source fetched reported deaths.

incidents.cause_summary: ASDSO: one of the 1977 inflatable Fabridams in the enlarged spillway collapsed after clean knife-cut slits; Colorado DWR and the manufacturer called it vandalism.
incidents.what_happened: During a late-night inspection on 17 March 1979, Consolidated Mutual Water Company staff found a Fabridam in the Maple Grove spillway collapsing and releasing the reservoir down Lena Gulch. About 2,000 people were evacuated along 2.3 miles of Lena Gulch in Wheat Ridge. About 100 acre-feet released over 2.5–3 hours (reservoir down about 3 feet); peak below the dam about 600 cfs. Basement and commercial flooding, bank and street damage. ASDSO: no life loss reported; evacuees returned at 4:20 a.m. on 18 March. Investigations found clean slits and a circular hole; the manufacturer’s engineer listed other U.S. Fabridam knife-cuts. The bag was patched and later water-filled; fencing, lighting and a low-pressure alarm were added.
incidents.status: Fabridam repaired 1979; dam remains in service (Consolidated Mutual)

incidents.what_happened: On 18–19 August 2007, remnants of Tropical Depression Erin dropped an estimated 8.3 inches in about six hours above Sugar Creek L-44, a 1971 NRCS flood-retarding dam reclassified high-hazard in 2005. The auxiliary spillway ran 2.6–3.6 feet deep. incidents.what_happened: On 4 April 1929 the Briseis Dam on the Cascade River above Derby, Tasmania — built to supply water for hydraulic tin mining — failed after unprecedented rain. incidents.what_happened: The original Eildon (Sugarloaf) rockfill dam on the Goulburn River first filled in August 1927. On 26 April 1929 evidence of failure was observed: more than 350 m of upstream rockfill slumped and the concrete core cracked (contemporary board of inquiry / later engineering papers). Independent hydrologist said operators achieved close to the best possible flood-mitigation result. 59% of downstream flooding was from dam releases (QFCI / Babister).
incidents.what_happened: In January 2011 Wivenhoe Dam recorded its largest inflows. Wikipedia: on 11 January the reservoir reached 191% of normal water-supply storage (60 cm below the auxiliary spillway). The Queensland Floods Commission of Inquiry found the flood engineers did not comply with the Wivenhoe/Somerset operations manual in the lead-up to the peak, while the Commission's hydrologist Mark Babister said they achieved close to the best possible flood-mitigation result and that 59% of downstream flooding was caused by water released from the dam. The Crime and Misconduct Commission later found no basis for charging the engineers. The embankment did not fail. Queensland 2010–11 flood deaths are not copied onto this record.
incidents.status: Dam held. Operating rules and the flood manual were reviewed after the inquiry.

incidents.cause_summary: ISSMGE Kristinsson et al.: during first impounding in August 1976, leakage far above design entered the dam body from pervious lava-flow abutments; high pore pressure; filling stopped. Leakage later reduced from >20 m³/s to about 6 m³/s by sealing and self-sealing.
incidents.what_happened: The Sigalda asphalt-faced rockfill dam on the Tungnaá was completed in late 1975. During first impounding in August 1976, ISSMGE (Kristinsson et al., ECSMGE 2019) report leakage much larger than expected through pervious postglacial lava-flow abutments; water entered the rockfill and pore pressure rose, so filling was stopped. The reservoir could not be filled to spillway level until sealing works; it reached spillway crest in 1980. Over 40 years leakage fell from more than 20 m³/s to about 6 m³/s. The dam remained stable. No sourced deaths.
incidents.status: First filling interrupted 1976; sealed; still operating (Landsvirkjun).

incidents.what_happened: El Cajón (Francisco Morazán), a 226 m double-curvature arch dam, developed large foundation leaks through limestone karst. The Inter-American Development Bank account: by 1993 water was entering the powerhouse at about 1,600 litres per second, discolored with clay. On 24 April 1994 a power surge knocked out electricity nationwide; the sump pumps stopped and emergency generators failed to start; geologist Jorge Flores said water nearly reached floor level before the turbines restarted and drove the pumps. IDB and ICOLD papers describe later grouting (including plastic/wooden balls and polypropylene sacks). The arch dam itself did not fail. No sourced deaths. Hurricane Mitch 1998 flood-control performance is a separate non-failure event and is not this record.

incidents.what_happened: Zaza, Cuba's largest reservoir, filled in weeks in May–June 1972 instead of the planned five years. Escambray's documented memoir: from 20 May to 17 June the reservoir gained more than 600 million m³; at about 18:30 on Saturday 17 June, while operators were closing the two valves on the underground pipes that had been feeding the Mapos rice scheme, a pipe ruptured and water, detachments and cracks opened in a stretch of the embankment slope. The leak was stopped on 24 June. The dam remains in service.

incidents.what_happened: On 17 June 2026, after a routine evening irrigation release of about 100,000 m³ from Mellègue (Nebeur) Dam toward Jendouba, the outlet gate — a 70-tonne gate in service since 1954 — left its axis while being closed (Faïez Msallem, Director-General of Dams, TAP/La Presse). incidents.what_happened: At about 06:00 local time on 19 October 2019 a process-pond dam on the Seiba River near Shchetinkino failed in heavy rain. BBC: at least 15 gold miners died and others were missing after water flooded workers' cabins; the regional head called the hydro-technical facility self-constructed and in violation of safety rules. DW/Interfax (20 Oct): Investigative Committee said the breach started at the highest of five illegal dams and a chain reaction broke four more; CEO, site chief and foreman of OOO Sisim (Sibzoloto holding) detained; 16 injured. German Wikipedia later listed 15 dead plus 6 missing.
incidents.status: Historical illegal cascade failure; criminal case opened.

sources.label: BBC — Russia dam collapse at Siberia gold mine kills 15

incidents.cause_summary: German Wikipedia / Adams (1984): the nearly finished Sienese gravity dam was already in poor condition; a written distress call of 4 December 1492 said it was about to break, and it failed in the last days of December.
incidents.what_happened: The Republic of Siena began a gravity dam on the Bruna near Giuncarico in 1470 to create a fish-stocking lake (Lago di Pietra). German Wikipedia, following Adams (Technology and Culture, 1984) and Farinelli/Francovich: the wall was up to 18 m high, 12 m at the base, 6 m at the crest and about 300 m long. Design changes and extra stone were needed from 1471; overtopping damaged the downstream face in the 1470s. A last written call for Francesco di Giorgio Martini on 4 December 1492 said the dam was in great danger. It broke in the last days of December 1492, flooding the Maremma. People and animals died; no source fetched gives a death count. Rebuild plans (including Baldassare Peruzzi) were never carried out. Ruins remain on the Gavorrano–Roccastrada boundary.
incidents.status: Failed 1492; ruins still visible. Not rebuilt.

incidents.cause_summary: ORF / South Tyrol provincial geologist Volkmar Mair: a mild autumn left ice-filled rock joints unfrozen; the 10,000 m³ pond drained through the fractured bedrock. Officials ruled out a construction defect.
incidents.what_happened: On 27 December 2011 (ORF: Tuesday shortly before 17:30) the warden of the Schöne Aussicht hut reported that a snowmaking pond at about 2,800 m on the Schnalstal glacier was losing water. About 10,000 m³ drained; the Schnalser Bach overflowed, muddied the valley ski run at three places, flooded the road in front of hotels in Kurzras, and three hotels were evacuated. ORF: no deaths or injuries. Provincial geologist Volkmar Mair attributed the leak to an extremely mild autumn so that normally ice-filled joints in the fractured rock did not freeze, plus heat from the pond; he thought slow subsurface leakage had already been going on for days. Wildbachverbauung and water-works officials said the basin itself was intact and excluded construction defects. German Wikipedia lists the event under dam-installation accidents.
incidents.status: Pond drained 2011; valley run later reopened. No deaths.

incidents.what_happened: The 16th-century buttress/earthfill dam of the Mar de Ontígola (about 140–150 m long, 6 m high) above Aranjuez overtopped during a 9 September 1990 cloudburst. El País (10 September 1990): the wetland south of and above the town 'desbordó el dique de contención'; a torrent of water and mud crossed the historic centre, flooded the national-police building (seven patrol cars), the municipal library and ground floors, and ponded up to a metre in places. Madrid–south road and rail links were cut. El País does not describe a masonry collapse. Madrid Ciudadanía y Patrimonio later said the spillways were not prepared for a flood; a 2020 Aranjuez plenary cited masonry-buttress problems that had already caused important 1990 flooding. No source fetched reported deaths.
incidents.status: Dam still stands; Hispania Nostra red-list heritage structure with later instability warnings (2011 type-A classification later revised).

incidents.what_happened: Alto Ceira I was a thin concrete arch finished in 1949 on the Ceira (Structurae: works 1940–49; 40°11′20.5″N 7°50′50.31″W). incidents.cause_summary: Vionnet et al. 2006: the west side of Santa Fe was suddenly flooded when a protective levee failed during the record Salado flood. Aletheia: water entered on 29 April through the unfinished Tramo 3 gap.
incidents.what_happened: At the end of April 2003 the Salado rose rapidly after heavy rain. Wikipedia flood page: on 28 April the river overflowed; about 100,000 people were evacuated and the page gives a flood-wide death figure of 154. Vionnet, Tassi, Rodríguez and Ferreira (IJRBM 2006) model the city flooding after a protective levee failed: about 120,000 people were suddenly displaced, 23 people died as a direct result of the flood, and 43 more are believed to have died from post-traumatic distress. Aletheia (UNLP): on 29 April water entered the city where Tramo 3 of a planned defence had not been finished, leaving 23 official deaths and more than 130,000 evacuees, with about one third of the city under water. CONICET/CIMEC papers describe an unfinished gap on the order of 150 m. This record uses the dated official-direct figure of 23 from Vionnet 2006 / Aletheia; Wikipedia's 154 is a flood-wide total and is not treated as this levee's isolated toll.
incidents.status: Unfinished defence overtopped/failed April 2003; later works completed the western front.

incidents.what_happened: On 22 May 2008 the two 8 m × 8 m horseshoe-shaped reinforced-concrete conduits that form Massingir Dam's bottom outlet works suffered a bursting failure. International Water Power (and the same article on NS Energy): reservoir level was 122.4 m, 7.4 m above the gated spillway sill, after crest gates had been installed a few years earlier — the highest hydrostatic pressure the conduits had seen. The right-hand downstream radial gate had been closed about six hours earlier. The paper attributes the failure to deficient reinforcement detailing that let pore pressure pull tensile steel from the curved faces. Zutari, later appointed for rehabilitation: sudden failure of the outlet conduits caused an uncontrolled discharge of about 1,000 m³/s and threatened the dam's structural safety. Demolition of loose concrete began in October 2008. No source fetched reported deaths from this outlet failure. Wikipedia gives the dam coordinates and 46 m height; Zutari gives 48 m and a 4.8 km crest.
incidents.status: Outlet works failed 2008; later rehabilitated (steel liners / radial-gate works reported by Zutari and ATB).

incidents.cause_summary: WA Ecology notable-failures list: excessive seepage through a glacial-moraine abutment caused a mudflow about one mile from the reservoir and destroyed the railroad and the village of Eastwick/Edgewick.
incidents.what_happened: About 2 a.m. on 23 December 1918, floodwater seeped through glacial debris near Seattle’s Cedar River / Masonry Dam and wiped out the logging town of Edgewick (also called Eastwick in later Ecology lists). Seattle Times: no one died; at least 12 families lost homes and belongings. Wikipedia: the town was completely destroyed in the dam-related burst known locally as the Boxley Blowout. WA Ecology: seepage through the glacial-moraine abutment; railroad line and village destroyed. The concrete Masonry Dam itself did not collapse.
incidents.status: historical / Edgewick later partly resettled, then destroyed again in 1932

incidents.what_happened: On the afternoon of 15 May 1936 the 10 m Campbell Meadows dam on the headwaters of Shuttleworth Creek failed (Penticton Herald 1936; Septer 2006; Tannant & Skermer, CGJ 2013). The earthfill dam, built in 1935 to store 1.2 million m³ for late-summer irrigation, had been weakened by two days of intermittent heavy rain. It did not overtop — water never rose within 1.2 m of the crest. About 123 000 m³ was released. Floodwater inundated farms at Okanagan Falls, demolished houses, drowned livestock, destroyed more than 1.6 km of highway and a small bridge, damaged orchards, and cut the Penticton–Oliver rail line and the main highway from the south. CGJ: no fatalities.
incidents.status: Rebuilt after 1936; failed again 27 May 1944 and was not rebuilt.

incidents.cause_summary: ASDSO/USACE case study: Maria spillway flows undermined chute slabs on a landslide foundation, leaving a large scour hole in the lower spillway. Main embankment did not breach. NWS/Governor 22 Sep 2017: ~70 000 downstream urged to evacuate.
incidents.what_happened: Hurricane Maria made landfall over Puerto Rico on 20 September 2017. On 22 September at 18:10 GMT operators announced the Guajataca Dam spillway was failing (Wikipedia; NWS). Governor Rosselló estimated close to 70 000 people could be affected if the dam collapsed and ordered evacuation. ASDSO/USACE: hydraulic-fill embankment (1928) on an active landslide complex; spillway flows exploited alignment and slab defects, head-cut the foundation, failed chute slabs, and left a scour hole hundreds of feet long and tens of feet deep in the lower chute; a 54-inch water siphon was severed. The main embankment did not fully breach. USACE emergency stabilization followed; Wikipedia: first-phase repairs to avoid flooding were completed 17 November 2017. No sourced death count at this dam. Island-wide Maria deaths are not copied here.
incidents.status: Spillway partially failed; main embankment held. USACE IRRM / emergency repairs; longer-term rehab ongoing after 2017.

incidents.cause_summary: Wikipedia (1931 China floods): after months of Yangtze–Huai high water, a typhoon on 24–25 August drove Grand Canal / Gaoyou Lake water through the dikes near Gaoyou Lake. AboutGaoyou: typhoon waves on the already-swollen suspended lake gouged the earthen canal levees.
incidents.what_happened: Wikipedia (1931 China floods): one of the disaster's worst single events was on 25 August 1931, when water rushing through the Grand Canal washed away dikes near Gaoyou Lake. In Gaoyou County alone it records 18,000 people drowned and 58,000 later deaths from famine and disease the following year. The AboutGaoyou reconstruction (Harnsberger family / Wang Shuxiang account) dates the early-morning cuts to 26 August, names the largest break Dang Jun Lou (about 550 m), and says six holes opened in the Gaoyou levees. A 2022 Gaoyou Daily reading of the 1933 Jiangbei Canal dike-break stele says at dawn on the 26th Gaoyou and Jiangdu Shaobo had 27 cuts totalling 880 zhang, of which six (460 zhang) were in Gaoyou — Dangjunlou, Miaoxiang, Qigongdian, Yumatou, plus Ershilipu and Sanshilipu. Harnsberger and Wang later rebuilt the dikes over about nine months. National 1931 flood totals are not copied onto this named levee.
incidents.status: Levees rebuilt 1931–32 (Harnsberger / Wang).

incidents.cause_summary: NDSA (SANDRP / Hindustan Times): pier settlement from a combination of planning, design, quality-control and O&M defects; later reporting also describes piping under the raft and inadequate geotechnical investigation.
incidents.what_happened: On the night of 21 October 2023 piers of the Lakshmi (Medigadda) barrage on the Godavari — the first barrage of the Kaleshwaram project at Medigadda village, Mahadevpur, Jayashankar Bhupalpally — sank. NDSA's 22 October order (SANDRP) said pillars 15–20 of blocks 6–8 had sunk and treated the event as a major dam failure under Dam Safety Act Schedule II para 8. Wikipedia: staff reported pillar 19 damaged and the bridge sagging, with pillars 20 and 21 also cracked. L&T built the 1,632 m barrage (85–86 gates) in 2019. A six-member NDSA committee visited; SANDRP's 3 Nov 2023 wrap and a 22 Oct 2024 Hindustan Times follow-up say the barrage was damaged by defects in planning, design, quality control and management and remained unrepaired a year later. No death count is given.
incidents.status: Piers settled; barrage out of normal service pending rehabilitation (HT Oct 2024).

incidents.cause_summary: Japanese Wikipedia / Dampedia / Kyoto DPRI: Tainter gate No. 3 failed about a month after completion; investigation attributed collapse to insufficient strength of the gate legs (buckling) and design that omitted hydrodynamic load. incidents.what_happened: Japanese Wikipedia and Mainichi (50-years-ago, 2017): on 2 July 1967, during heavy rain that rapidly raised the new Kansai Electric Wachi Dam on the Yura, the third gate blew out. Mainichi: the 35-tonne gate was carried about 100 m downstream; two ayu anglers were swept away and one body was found the next day. Dampedia: peak release about 780 m³/s; one angler died. Japanese Wikipedia cites Asahi 3 July 1967 ('new dam gate blown, evacuation warning') and 26 July 1967 ('lightweight gate / cheap construction'). Construction Ministry and MITI set up the Wachi Dam Gate Accident Technical Investigation Committee chaired by Yano Katsumasa (Kyoto DPRI). The dam (gravity concrete, 25.2 m, 5.119 million m³) later entered service in 1968 after gate reconstruction.
incidents.status: Gate replaced; dam in service (Kansai Electric).

incidents.cause_summary: Oberbergmeister Ey / Martin Schmidt: a cavity from internal erosion of a damaged turf-sod seal, without wave-protection riprap, opened a hole on the downstream face and the dam collapsed in fair weather at normal water.
incidents.what_happened: German Wikipedia: the dam (about 110 m long, 6 m high, built around 1620) failed unexpectedly on the afternoon of 29 September 1820 in good weather at normal storage. Witness Böhler saw a large hole open on the air-side slope and the dam collapse seconds later. Woodcutter Papst had seen a hole in the crest the day before that gurgled and grew. The breach was about 20 m (11–12 Lachter) wide. Ey concluded the turf-sod seal was defective and lacked riprap, and that a cavity had grown inside until collapse. Person or property damage from the wave is not documented. The pond was not rebuilt; a shallow wetland remains at the listed ruin on the Harzwasserwerke 'Einersberger Teiche' water walk.

incidents.what_happened: German Wikipedia: the municipal Neuer Teich on the Münzbach southeast of Freiberg-Neusorge was built 1674–1682 as a process-water pond (also feeding the Kuhschacht art ditch). On the evening of 1 June 1839, after heavy rain, the Berthelsdorfer Hüttenteich spillways were opened and water plus hillside runoff filled the Neuer Teich. About 03:00 on 2 June, Kunststeiger Müller found floodwater at Vorwerk A.B.C. and could not open the Neuer Teich Fluter because it was nailed; he went for help. About 04:00 the dam broke and a flood wave ran down the Freiberger Münzbachtal. The city later left the site waste ('Ausgerissener Teich'); a 1902 development plan used that name. No death count in the sources fetched.
incidents.status: Not rebuilt as a reservoir; site later urbanised as Ausgerissener Teich.

incidents.cause_summary: German Wikipedia: the 6 m earth dam (1906), with no bottom outlet, overtopped unnoticed in a cloudburst and then breached about 30 m.
incidents.what_happened: German Wikipedia: after two days of rain, a thunderstorm dropped 80 mm in two hours on the Süntel on 19 July 1966. The 1906 detention basin about 300 m above Fischbeck (no Grundablass) overtopped about an hour after the storm began, then breached about 30 m around 18:50 (Hamburger Abendblatt) or 21:00 (another cited source), releasing about 164,000 m³ as a roughly 4 m wave. About 1,000 residents reached upper floors; 150 houses in Fischbeck were damaged (50 severely, 5 destroyed); livestock losses were high. Wikipedia and the Heimatverein: no human deaths at Fischbeck (one storm death at Arzell in North Hesse is a different place). The dam was later raised to 11.90 m (1968/69 and 1999) with a controlled outlet; capacity now about 935,000 m³.
incidents.status: Rebuilt higher with outlet and alarm; in service.

About 18.3 GL flowed through the opening and caused severe damage to all towns downstream. The first Loddon bridge at Laanecoorie (1870) was destroyed with the weir. John Monash later designed a reinforced-concrete replacement bridge that remains in use. Spillway extensions were completed in 1909 and the spillway was raised to its current height in 1935. Goulburn-Murray Water operates the storage. Wikipedia and the ANCOLD register row cited there do not give a death count.
incidents.status: Rebuilt / operational (Goulburn-Murray Water).

incidents.what_happened: Rum Jungle uranium mill opened 1954 on the East Branch of the Finniss River. IAEA/Waggitt: tailings were discharged to a dam on a flat part of the site; over time about 150,000 t were lost from the dam to the adjacent river through overtopping by supernatant flow and wet-season rainfall. National Museum of Australia: from the start of processing, tailings discharged freely; later attempts at containing or diluting them were inadequate and wet-season spills into the East Branch continued; about 640,000 t of tailings had been discharged by the 1970s; about 100 km² of floodplains affected. APH/Mudd compilation: Acid and Sweetwater retention dams on the Finniss were built in 1961 and regularly overflowed. Rehabilitation 1982–86 placed remnant tailings into Dyson's pit. No death count. The water damaged an internal farm road, hit a sugar-cane plantation and surrounded houses. Nobody was injured. Igarn said the dam was not in SNISB and ordered halt of unlicensed reconstruction (no Licença de Obra Hidráulica). Witnesses told Inter TV Cabugi the dam had cracks days earlier and had been enlarged about two months before.
incidents.status: Ruptured 26 July 2026; unlicensed rebuild halted by Igarn.

Villagers noticed a small hole on the evening of 12 August; officials could not plug it; the leak widened to about 20 feet overnight. incidents.what_happened: NIDM (quoted by DeshGujarat, 11 Sept 2024): Pratappura dam (also Pratapsingh Tank), about 4,040 acres catchment, 7 gates; a 50-metre-wide breach on Friday 1 July 2005 inundated five nearby villages and sent a large flow into Vadodara. DeshGujarat local-daily recap: seven villages vacated (Shankarpura, Bodindra, Jarod, Paldi, Hansapura, Pratappura, Panch Devla); 12 inch overnight rain at Pratappura; the 2005 breach was reportedly at the same place as the 2001 100 m breach. No death count is given for this named dam; Gujarat/Vadodara 2005 flood totals (ReliefWeb 108 then 132 statewide) are not copied. Distinct from CWC 2001 and the 13 August 2012 partial breach.
incidents.status: Breached 1 July 2005; later X-ray study and strengthening (NIDM via DeshGujarat).

incidents.cause_summary: Gansu reinforcement tender: the auxiliary dam was overtopped and failed in 1979. A desert-climate account: July 1979 snowmelt plus concentrated rain; flood gates were not opened; the dam broke on 26 July.
incidents.what_happened: The Danghe Reservoir (construction started 1971; first stage in service 1975) lost its auxiliary dam in 1979. A Gansu provincial reinforcement tender states the auxiliary dam was overtopped and failed in 1979, then the works were raised and repeatedly strengthened. Dunhuang media: 1979–1980 auxiliary-dam rebuild among seven construction stages. A popular climate/history account dates the break to 26 July 1979 after the reservoir was held full (snowmelt plus abnormal rain; gates not opened) and says six townships and 21 villages were flooded and Dunhuang city was inundated; it does not give a death count. Present works: asphalt-concrete-core gravel dams; main dam 56.8 m; total storage 46.40 million m³.
incidents.status: Auxiliary dam rebuilt 1979–80; later raised and reinforced.

incidents.what_happened: On 27 June 1994 an erosion sinkhole opened in the original about 200-foot phosphogypsum stack at IMC-Agrico's New Wales plant in Polk County, Florida. FDEP/Earthdoc: the depression was observed 185 feet deep and 120 feet wide, with a 480-foot conduit to the Upper Floridan aquifer. Ardaman: plant production wells pumping on the order of 8 million gallons per day were used as recovery wells and the papers state contamination was contained on the plant site; more than 3,800 cubic yards of pea-gravel concrete were injected about 400 feet beneath the stack surface. IMC spent about $7 million on exploration and remediation. No source fetched gave a death count or a released-volume figure comparable to the 2016 Mosaic sinkhole. The 27 August 2016 Mosaic New Wales sinkhole is a separate record.
incidents.status: historical / original stack throat grouted; 2016 sinkhole is a later event at the same plant

incidents.cause_summary: USACE / FEMA / Wikipedia: after a record flood pool in January 2009, two depressions, muddy seepage and high flow through the right abutment indicated possible internal erosion. Not a breach.
incidents.what_happened: This is an incident, not a confirmed breach. On 9 January 2009 Howard A. Hanson Dam reached a record pool of 1,189 feet after inflows peaked at 30,500 cfs. USACE then found two depressions on the right abutment, sediment-laden water in the drainage tunnel, and higher-than-expected seepage. On 16 January USACE reduced the rated pool from 1,206 to 1,155 feet. FEMA appeal narrative and Wikipedia: interim seepage barrier and drainage work were in place by November 2009; well and drainage-tunnel work finished November 2011; the dam was later returned toward full flood storage. USACE estimated the January 2009 operation prevented about $3.9–4 billion in downstream damages. No source fetched treated this as a breach or gave a death count.
incidents.status: incident / abutment grouted and drainage improved; dam remains in service

incidents.cause_summary: ARIA 39622: about 24 h of overtopping on 160 m of crest after rain and snowmelt; no spillway and undersized gates. The dam did not rupture.
incidents.what_happened: ARIA (night 6–7 January 2011, Anor): the 8 ha / 300,000 m³ Étang de Neuve Forge rose rapidly after rain and snowmelt. The 17th-century earth dam, straddling Anor and Hirson, overtopped for nearly 24 h over almost the entire 160 m embankment (water blade more than 10 cm). Overtopping eroded the fill in five places several metres wide; at the outlet, only an unexplained concrete wall still held. Firefighters evacuated 6 people and 10 horses from a stud immediately below. Prefectoral order of 1 March cancelled the dam authorisation and required a lower water level. The owner began works in February 2012. No death count is given.
incidents.status: Overtopping contained; authorisation cancelled March 2011; works 2012.

incidents.what_happened: ARIA (9 June 2018, Le Genest-Saint-Isle): during a flood, overtopping of a pond ruined the crest and downstream slope of an earth dam and flooded the bourg and primary school. The dam remained at risk of rupture; houses in the inundation path were evacuated. Four days later the pond was only 70 cm lower. Control officers found many internal seepage paths; the owner had plugged an active leak with demolition rubble and boarded the spillway 40 cm higher. A prefectoral order required an official 1.5 m trench (cut 12 June). France 3 later: 1.80 m of water in the school; no victims. ICI: étang de la Pelleterie at La Pelluère, about 8,000 m², was the main threat in the following days. Ouest-France: 28 houses evacuated 11 June as a precaution.
incidents.status: Crest ruined 9 June; official trench cut from 12 June 2018.

incidents.geo_source: Nominatim (Diga di Palagnedra). Wikipedia Lago di Palagnedra 46°9′34″N 8°37′37″E is the reservoir.

incidents.cause_summary: ASDSO / damfailures.org: flood debris blocked the 13 spillway openings and the dam overtopped; the dam itself did not fail.
incidents.what_happened: ASDSO case study (Palagnedra Dam, Switzerland, 1978): the 72 m concrete gravity-arch dam, finished 1952, was overtopped on 7 August 1978 when about 25,000 m³ of wood debris blocked the 13 spillway openings. The diversion tunnel had been closed at police request to delay flooding of a campground about 10 km downstream. Overtopping on the right abutment eroded earthen backfill and exposed the concrete core. About 1.8 million m³ of sediment covered the diversion tunnel 12–14 m deep. The dam did not collapse. damfailures.org: the flood on the Melezza killed 24 people upstream of the facility — that upstream flood toll is not copied onto this dam record. The incident drove later Swiss spillway-debris rules.
incidents.status: Dam survived; spillway/debris rules later tightened.

incidents.cause_summary: BBC 3 Sep 2011: after six hours of torrential rain the dam overflowed. World Bank IUFMP / FUNAAB: dam remained stable; stilling basin and downstream walls damaged; waterworks submerged.
incidents.what_happened: On Friday 26 August 2011, after hours of torrential rain, Eleyele Dam on the Ona River in Ibadan overflowed. BBC (3 September 2011): Ibadan Water Corporation's Oguntola Gabriel said the water exceeded the dam's capacity so the rest had to overflow, and that this last happened in 1980; BBC described water pouring over the top near midnight. France 24 / AFP (1 September 2011) quoted Nigerian Red Cross disaster coordinator Umar Mairiga saying the dam 'collapsed' and giving a then death toll of 102; BBC two days later wrote that more than 120 people perished. Later technical assessments do not treat the embankment as having breached: a FUNAAB paper on the 26 August flood said the dam was stable but the stilling basin and downstream walls were damaged and the waterworks, transformer, pump house and control panels were completely submerged as water rose about 2.4 m above the channel floor; the paper said spillway capacity was adequate and findings went contrary to the belief that upper-catchment dams 'gave up'. An IDRiM 2012 paper likewise called stilling-basin and wing-wall damage a secondary cause of the city flood. German Wikipedia: the 26 August 2011 flood heavily damaged the works; Oyo State later rehabilitated the dam and intake tower under the World Bank IUFMP (works released 2018). World Bank IUFMP ESIA: earth dam built 1942, reservoir 7 Mm³, embankment 244 m (138 m plus 106 m spillway), crest height 13.0 m, ungated ogee spillway design flood 367.9 m³/s. Deaths left null: contemporaneous Red Cross/BBC figures are Ibadan flood totals attributed to the overflow; later papers say the dam did not collapse and the city flood had multiple causes (blocked drains, building on waterways). Those city-wide counts are not copied onto the dam.
incidents.status: Spillway/stilling basin damaged 2011; dam and intake tower later rehabilitated under IUFMP (Oyo State 2018).

incidents.cause_summary: UBRBDA: embankment overtopped and breached about 200 m of 1,300 m in 1998 from inadequate spillway capacity. Umaru et al. / IJERT: overtopped by a flash flood; unfinished spillway; design crest not reached at 1992 commissioning.
incidents.what_happened: Upper Benue River Basin Development Authority: Cham Dam was built 1982–1990 by direct labour for flood control on the Gombe–Yola highway, plus water supply and about 200 ha irrigation. The embankment overtopped and breached a section of about 200 m out of a total length of 1,300 m in 1998 because of inadequate spillway capacity. Umaru, Choji and Mshelia (ARPN JEAS 2010 / IJERT): Cham multipurpose earth dam in Cham village, Gombe, storage about 8 million m³, commissioned December 1992, failed September 1998; two conflicting cross-section designs existed and the built section was a homogeneous mismatched fill; spillway not completed; design height not achieved when hurriedly commissioned. The dam failed hydraulically and structurally when overtopped; the breach cut to foundation level. Punch later reported FEC approval of N612 million to complete rehabilitation, the minister saying the 1982 dam was breached after unprecedented rainfall and inadequate spillways. No sourced death count for the 1998 breach.
incidents.status: Breached 1998 (~200 m of 1,300 m). Reconstruction contract awarded 2011; later RETC/FEC revisions reported.

incidents.what_happened: Japanese Wikipedia (夜明ダム): during the June 1953 West Japan flood (Chikugo basin more than 500 mm) the unfinished Kyushu Electric gravity dam had only 3 of 8 gates operable. Both banks overtopped and the works 'failed' (決壊); the body did not completely collapse, but equipment was damaged and washed out. A 1954 Fukuoka–Ōita joint 夜明ダム調査報告書, cited there, concluded downstream damage was from poor river works rather than a direct dam-break wave. Ōita CERD archive and Kyushu Electric construction-album captions place the flood at the dam in the 25–29 June 1953 event. No death count for the dam itself in the sources fetched. The dam was completed in May 1954 (height 15.0 m; 4.05 million m³; 12 MW Yoake power station).

incidents.what_happened: Japanese Wikipedia (荒砥沢ダム): at the 14 June 2008 Iwate–Miyagi inland earthquake a landslide about 1,300 m long, 900 m wide, 150 m scarp and about 67 million m³ (Wikipedia; PWRI 45 million m³ at an early Miyagi figure) entered Aizenko. A seiche overtopped the second service spillway (estimated more than 6 m) but did not overtop the crest; storage had been drawn down before the rainy season and the slide volume was about a tenth of storage. The dam settled but was not judged unstable. About 1.5 million m³ of sediment cut storage; MAFF built a 560,000 m³ substitute pond at Okitomi. Restoration finished in FY2011. No death count at the dam or this landslide in the sources fetched.
incidents.status: Dam remained; landslide is a Kurikoma Geopark / Japanese Geological 100 site. Substitute pond built.

incidents.status: Emergency rebuild then Yabe special-disaster and large-scale related projects.

incidents.cause_summary: Tropical wave 33 rain on 14–15 August 2002 overtopped and tore a large breach (boquete) in the 1848 masonry irrigation dam at La Ventilla. CNA satellite note: strongest activity 19:00 on 14 August to 06:00 on 15 August.
incidents.what_happened: On the night of 14–15 August 2002 the masonry irrigation dam at La Ventilla, Villa de Reyes, San Luis Potosí, failed in tropical-wave-33 rain. Protección Civil / CNA called the structure presa La Ventilla and said it was totally lost (CNA via La Jornada). President Fox visited the community on 16 August and stood at the large breach the water had torn in Presa Dolores (La Jornada 17 Aug). Governor Silva Nieto: the work dates from 1848; there had been an overflow in 1976, not of this size. El País (16 Aug), citing Gobernación spokesman Carlos Gelista: nine people from two families died in San Luis Potosí where La Ventilla overflowed; two people missing; 450 ha of crops damaged; four shelters for about 1,500. La Jornada: about 300 houses damaged and 600 people in shelters in Villa de Reyes. DOF FONDEN: atypical rains 14–16 August in Villa de Reyes. Statewide SLP+Zacatecas death totals are not copied onto this dam.
incidents.status: Failed August 2002 (large breach). Later local monitoring still refers to a Presa La Ventilla in Villa de Reyes.

incidents.cause_summary: La Jornada 2 June 2000: neighbours had reported wall fractures for more than three years; torrential rain from 21:00 on 31 May tore a section of the canal bordo.
incidents.what_happened: In the early hours of 1 June 2000 a levee of the Canal de La Compañía sewage-and-storm canal failed at Valle de Chalco, State of Mexico. La Jornada (2 June): rain from 21:00 on 31 May; about 5,000 people climbed onto roofs as water reached almost 2 m; a 7 m opening in the canal edge, and two fractures at El Molino, Ixtapaluca; main opening near km 27+600 of the Mexico–Puebla highway. Milenio (citing Protección Civil Edomex / CENAPRED): a 16 m fracture in the lower left bordo; DOF emergency for Chalco, Valle de Chalco and Ixtapaluca. CNDH Recomendación 16/2000 opened an ex officio file on the 1 June bordo rupture. Academic review (Aragón-Durand 2009 via SciELO): 80 ha flooded; more than 6,700 households affected. No sourced death count for this levee.
incidents.status: Levee repaired; canal later piped. Failed again in February 2010 (separate record).

incidents.cause_summary: Mine workers (La Jornada 16 Aug 2010): part of the old tailings-dam curtain collapsed the night of 7 August; they said they had warned the dam was poorly designed and managers only ordered desilting.
incidents.what_happened: On the night of 7 August 2010 part of the curtain of the old tailings dam at the Bolaños silver-gold mine, Bolaños, Jalisco, collapsed into the Río Bolaños. La Jornada 16 Aug (workers / Grupo México mine): the old dam held about 2 million tonnes; employees said about 400,000 tonnes had entered the river by that Sunday. Gaceta UDG: rupture on Sunday 8 August of a Minerales y Minas Mexicanas dam, 300,000 tonnes, carried 32 km; UAG lab the next day reported lead 479.08 ppm vs NOM-127 0.025, arsenic 0.45 vs 0.05, mercury 0.14 vs 0.001. Municipal president López Raygoza (Agustín del Castillo): company estimate at least 150,000 tonnes of 20-year-old stored material, reaching past San Martín de Bolaños; fish kill, no cattle deaths reported to him. PROFEPA later said accredited tests were below limits and still opened a case for the abandoned dam (about 300,000 tonnes of mud). No sourced human death count.
incidents.status: Old TSF curtain failed August 2010; PROFEPA required stabilization and an abandonment programme.

incidents.what_happened: On 14 March 1979 the Petatlán earthquake (M 7.6) shook CFE's El Infiernillo (Adolfo López Mateos) rockfill dam on the Balsas (149 m, opened 1965). Reséndiz, Romo and Moreno, Journal of the Geotechnical Engineering Division 108(1) 1982: measurable deformations in both Infiernillo and La Villita, including settlement, slope distortion and cracking; accelerations were recorded on rock and on the embankments. The paper does not describe a breach or loss of the reservoir. No sourced death count for the dam.
incidents.status: Remained in service. Further seismic deformation in 1985 (separate record).

incidents.what_happened: Folha de S.Paulo (5 February 2004): a dike holding the Poti and Parnaíba in low Teresina had part of its structure undermined by rain. A 20 m hole at the base, caused by erosion, enlarged and let water into riverside streets, mainly Mocambinho and Poty Velho, which had already been flooding for about 15 days. Defesa Civil technical adviser Espedito Soares Cavalcante said a larger disaster was avoided because residents had been removed and the rivers had dropped about 40 cm. It had shown rupture signs since the start of the week; Defesa Civil and the prefecture tried cement barriers and stakes but the undermining still occurred. Maintenance crews were working to contain the flow. Statewide Piauí rain losses (~50,000 people) are not copied onto this dike. The 1985 Teresina flood itself is ordinary river flooding (not a structure failure) and is not this record.

incidents.what_happened: On 11 February 2025 rustic containment barriers at an illegal gold garimpo (São Domingos / Igarapé Água Preta, Pedra Branca do Amapari) ruptured and sent mining sediment into the Cupixi, then the Amapari and Araguari. incidents.cause_summary: Agência Brasil: the gate was partly closed on 23 August 2017 because of an electrical problem, interrupting flow for about 24 hours.
incidents.what_happened: Agência Brasil: closing the gates of the Paranã dam in Goiás left the river bed dry for about 24 hours. The state secretariat that operates the dam (SED) said the gate was partly closed on the 23rd because of an electrical problem; flow fell substantially the next day and was reopened in the afternoon; water only reached near Flores de Goiás on the 25th. The dam safety plan was activated. Ibama inspectors visited; SED said the volume of dead fish did not amount to a 'disaster or large environmental impact.' ANA has jurisdiction because the Paranã is a federal river. ANA Resolução 551/2004 pins the reservoir at 14°42′07″S 47°16′45″W and sets minimum downstream flows. Menescal's January 2005 'Paranã / Flores de Goiás / population insecurity' row is not used as a separate rupture — no primary 2005 rupture article was found.
incidents.status: 23 August 2017 electrical gate-closure incident; river dry ~24 h.

incidents.what_happened: Harju Elu and ERR: water disappeared from the Kotka weir pond on the Valgejõgi in Kuusalu on 7 August 2016 (ERR published 9 August). Environment Board specialist Rein Urman said the poorly maintained structure failed when timber support posts broke under water pressure; the owner (AS Generaator) filed a police report alleging vandalism. The weir dates to a 1950s hydro rebuild on a ~150-year mill site; generation (~200 kW) had been restored in 1994. No death count is given.

incidents.what_happened: On 28 October 1990 a dam at the Brewer Gold Mine near Jefferson, South Carolina, failed after large rainstorms. EPA Superfund profile and Five-Year Review: more than 10 million gallons of cyanide solution from a plastic-lined pond flowed into Little Fork Creek; fish were killed in the creek and for nearly 50 miles down the Lynches River. incidents.what_happened: On 17 June 2024 the St. Mary Canal siphon about eight miles north of Babb, Montana, failed. Reclamation: at about 8:45 a.m. a siphon barrel breached with about 600 cfs in the canal; washouts 30-50 ft deep; diversions from the St. Mary River to the Milk River were stopped. Montana Free Press / Milk River Joint Board: Reclamation had been monitoring a crack; the pair of 90-inch riveted-steel barrels (about 3200-3600 ft across the St. Mary valley) failed — one in the morning, the second about five hours later — and the inlets also gave way; Hook's Hide-Away bar, hotel and roping arena on Camp 9 Road were significantly impacted; no one was hurt. The 1915 canal supplies most Milk River Project irrigation (about 120000 acres) and municipal water. No source fetched gave a death other than the Board no one was hurt.
incidents.status: siphon destroyed; replacement designed 2024-25 (HDR / Reclamation / Milk River Joint Board)

incidents.cause_summary: EA: first-filling leakage through the asphaltic concrete membrane near the draw-off culvert (1975–80); January 2001 toe spring of about 15 l/s from aged membrane cracks forced a full drawdown.
incidents.what_happened: Winscar is a 53 m rockfill dam with an upstream asphaltic-concrete membrane, completed 1975 (first major UK dam of this type). Charles, Tedd and Warren (EA 2011) record first-filling leakage from differential settlement at the culvert collar, grouting 1978–80, and a full-depth membrane crack. In January 2001 a large spring of about 15 l/s appeared at the toe; New Civil Engineer (17 May 2001) quoted Yorkshire Water's Jim Claydon that seepage fell once the reservoir was 22 m down, pointing to a membrane defect. Wikipedia and Claydon's 2002 case study: the reservoir was emptied over about six months; a PVC geomembrane was installed and works finished March 2002. Dam stability was not threatened. No deaths.

incidents.cause_summary: EA: catastrophic failure of scour pipework and an undersized butterfly-valve gearbox during commissioning tests, releasing water into the draw-off tower.
incidents.what_happened: Ogston is a 20 m puddle-clay-core embankment (completed 1959; EA capacity 6,180×10³ m³) on the River Amber. Charles, Tedd and Warren (EA 2011, incident 44, severity 1): during commissioning tests on a replacement butterfly valve, the pipework immediately upstream and the compensation branch suffered catastrophic flange fractures. Water filled the draw-off tower, where two men were operating the valve, then forced the tunnel doors and discharged to the tail-bay. The upstream guard valve was shut by men going back through the discharging water. Investigation: the gearbox was undersized and one of four coupling screws was missing; instantaneous valve closure produced surge estimated above 55 bar. Grey cast iron fractured at the flanges. No deaths.
incidents.status: Emergency isolation; temporary bulkhead and extra washout fitted during repairs.

incidents.cause_summary: EA: deep-seated slip in both shoulders in September 1941 from rapid wartime placement of boulder-clay fill before the dam reached design height.
incidents.what_happened: Muirhead (Paisley Corporation Water Works; Gazetteer for Scotland: 21 m earth embankment on the Rye Water, opened 1942) was being raised under wartime pressure. EA 2011 (incident 50): by September 1941 fill had reached 21 m of a planned 26 m. Noticeable deformations developed in both slopes with tension cracks about 6 m from the centre-line. Building Research Station investigation: the lower shoulder fill was at limiting equilibrium (average undrained strength about 40 kPa); adding 0.5 m of fill produced immediate outward movements. The bank was kept at 21 m and a substantial upstream berm added; the dam was completed November 1942. Knockendon, then at 6 m nearby, was redesigned with toe weighting. Gazetteer for Scotland independently notes a partial failure the year before completion. No deaths.
incidents.status: Completed 1942 at reduced height with an upstream berm; now Scottish Water.

incidents.name: Upper Glendevon Dam first-filling leakage and uplift
incidents.region: Glen Devon, Ochil Hills, Perth and Kinross, Scotland
incidents.location_label: Upper Glendevon Reservoir dam, Glen Devon, United Kingdom
incidents.geo_source: HES Trove Upper Glendevon Reservoir And Dam NN 9086 0454 / 56.22086, -3.76163
incidents.river_or_facility: Upper Glendevon Reservoir / River Devon headwaters
incidents.cause_summary: EA: first-filling leaks through monolith joints and a honeycombed mass-concrete gravity dam on brecciated andesite, with high uplift and no grout curtain.
incidents.what_happened: Upper Glendevon is a 45 m mass-concrete gravity dam in 24 monoliths, built 1950–55 for Fife Regional Council (EA capacity 5,040×10³ m³). Charles, Tedd and Warren (EA 2011, incident 95): during impounding in July 1954, water appeared in such quantity while the stilling basin was being built that sub-drainage was provided. Leakage through vertical joints reached 27 l/s by 1956; fluorescein showed flows through the concrete. High uplift forced emptying and grouting in 1959–60 (520 t curtain, 200 t blanket). In 1958 toe uplift reached about 40 per cent of full head. October 1969 leakage emerged in the river bed 30 m downstream. A four-metre top-water restriction (almost 30 per cent of usable storage) was imposed, lifted 1973 and re-imposed 1979 after a nearby tremor. 1992–94 remedial: a downstream rockfill embankment and new south spillway (MacDonald/Kerr/Johnston; Gazetteer for Scotland: £5.24 million, 280,000 m³ rockfill; reopened 26 October 1994). No deaths.
incidents.status: Strengthened with downstream rockfill 1994; in service (Scottish Water).

incidents.name: Mullardoch Dam gallery leakage and cracking
incidents.location_label: Mullardoch Dam, Glen Cannich, United Kingdom
incidents.geo_source: Historic Environment Scotland LB51703 NH 22241 31365
incidents.river_or_facility: Loch Mullardoch / River Cannich (Glen Affric hydro scheme)
incidents.cause_summary: EA: sudden rise in gallery leakage and opening of near-horizontal cracks from longitudinal compressive stress (calcite in joints plus valley closure) at the 140° central buttress.
incidents.what_happened: Mullardoch is a 730 m mass-concrete gravity dam of unusual arrowhead plan (two flanks meet at 140° at a central buttress), completed 1951 for the Glen Affric scheme (HES: 727 m long, 48 m high; EA sheet height 50 m, capacity 223,000×10³ m³). EA 2011 incident 97: on 4 July 1986 weekly surveillance found gallery leakage up from 0.16 l/s (25 June) to 5.2 l/s. Pre-existing near-horizontal gallery cracks had opened up to 1.5 mm, mainly in two blocks about 15 m either side of the buttress, with water issuing under pressure and a sharp rise in uplift. The reservoir was lowered 7 m within 24 hours. Gosschalk et al. (1991): 3-D modelling blamed build-up of longitudinal compression from calcium-carbonate deposition in vertical joints plus valley-side closure, tilting the central buttress under high temperature. Remedial: foundation drainage/pressure-relief holes and 26 restressable vertical tendons plus transverse gallery tendons on the four central blocks (Hinks et al., 1990; Hayward, NCE 25 Oct 1990). No deaths.
incidents.status: Post-tensioned 1986–90s; still in service (SSE).

incidents.geo_source: HES Trove Dundreggan Dam NH 35732 15646 / 57.20206, -4.72083
incidents.river_or_facility: Dundreggan Reservoir / River Moriston (Garry–Moriston scheme)
incidents.cause_summary: EA: a change in gate operation caused severe vibration at low openings; fatigue cracks formed in the vertical skin-plate stiffener webs of a radial flood gate.
incidents.what_happened: Dundreggan is a 16 m concrete gravity dam (completed 1957; EA capacity 1,640×10³ m³) on the River Moriston with two radial flood gates 8.25 m high by 8.69 m wide (HES: also a central drum gate; about 55 ft high). EA 2011 incident 99: after the Folsom (California) gate failure, Scottish Hydro-Electric inspected its gates. The left-bank radial gate was taken out of service in summer 1998 to fit self-lubricating trunnion bearings; inspection found cracks in the web of the vertical skin-plate stiffener beams. A change in operation had caused severe vibration at low openings and fatigue cracking. The gate-lip geometry was modified to give a clean flow separation (Lewin, 1995); vibration stopped. HES notes 1999 refurbishment. No reservoir release and no deaths.

incidents.cause_summary: EA: one of three major 1937 UK construction slips (with Abberton and Chingford); Bridle: sudden strain-softening clay-foundation failure during construction.
incidents.what_happened: Hollowell is a water-supply embankment in Northamptonshire (Wikipedia list: built 1936–39; SP 69000 72400). Charles, Tedd and Warren (EA 2011 §2.4): during 1937 major slips occurred at three embankment dams under construction — Abberton in July, Hollowell in October, and the better-known William Girling (Chingford) downstream slip at the end of July. Rodney Bridle (Ground Engineering, 2026 comment on White Horse Reservoir) groups Hollowell with Chingford, Abberton (1937) and Carsington (1984) as sudden construction failures in strain-softening clay foundation materials, with no prior movement. The reservoir was completed 1939 and remains in service. No reservoir was yet impounded at the slip; no deaths.

incidents.what_happened: Pentwyn (also Pen-twyn / Taff Fechan / Dol-y-gaer) is a 9.5–10 m puddle-clay-core embankment completed 1863 under Thomas Hawksley (Coflein: reservoir built 1858–62, dam about SO 055145).
